cards.text: Meet the Teacher, son of David, king in Jerusalem (Ecclesiastes 1:1). He's been taking a hard look at life under the sun, and now he's looking at all the work people do and all the success they chase. And he's got a theory about where all that hustle comes from.

cards.question: Where does the Teacher say all labor and success spring from?

answers.text: A man's envy of his neighbor
A man's love for his family
A man's fear of going hungry

cards.text: His verdict: "This too is futile and a pursuit of the wind." Your neighbor buys a boat, so you take a second job, and the poor man doesn't even KNOW he's in a race with you.

cards.question: So what about the man who just quits working? The fool folds his hands. What does the Teacher say the fool does?

cards.text: So it's not work yourself to the bone, and it's not do nothing either. The Teacher holds up a picture with handfuls in it.

cards.question: The Teacher compares handfuls. Which one does he say is better?

cards.text: One handful and peace. Friend, I will take ONE cookie in a quiet kitchen over two cookies with the smoke alarm SCREAMING at me.
Again, the Teacher sees futility under the sun. This time it's about one man and his work.

cards.question: Who does this hardworking man have in his life, according to the Teacher?

answers.text: A son to inherit it all

cards.question: There is no end to this man's labor, and his eyes are content with his wealth.
All alone and working without end, the man finally asks himself a question. What does he want to know?

answers.text: Who he is working so hard for
How he can earn even more

cards.text: He asks, "For whom do I toil and bereave my soul of enjoyment?" Biggest cookie jar on the whole block, and the man has never once taken a cookie out of it.

cards.question: What does the Teacher call this lonely man's endless work?

cards.text: After that lonely man, the Teacher lands the big one: "Two are better than one."

cards.question: Why does the Teacher say two are better than one?

answers.text: They have a good return for their labor
They can split the blame for mistakes
They never have to work very hard

cards.text: Then he paints three pictures of two people sticking together. Picture one: somebody falls down.

cards.question: When one of the two falls down, what can his companion do?

cards.text: But "pity the one who falls without another to help him up!" I tipped over in the back of that junk drawer once and stayed SIDEWAYS until somebody went digging for tape.

cards.question: Picture two: the Teacher says that if two lie down together, they will keep warm.
Picture three: the Teacher says that though one may be ___, two can resist.

cards.text: Two is good. But the Teacher isn't done counting, because now he brings out a cord of three strands.

cards.question: What does the Teacher say about a cord of three strands?

answers.text: It is too heavy to carry

cards.text: Now a royal matchup, starting with an old but foolish king who no longer knows how to take a warning. His check-engine light has been on so long he thinks it's DECORATION.

cards.question: Who does the Teacher say is better than an old but foolish king?

cards.text: And this youth did not come up the easy way. He was born poor in his own kingdom.

cards.question: Where did the poor youth come from to become king?
When the youth succeeded the king, all who lived and walked under the sun followed him.

cards.text: And the crowd? "There is no limit to all the people who were before them." From prison to the throne with everybody behind him, friend, now THAT is a comeback.

cards.question: The Teacher says the people who come even later will celebrate the youth who became king.

cards.text: Then that line again: "This too is futile and a pursuit of the wind." Today's big name is tomorrow's expired coupon, and believe me, I shared a drawer with one that STILL believed in itself.

findings.problem: Stop 2, card 1 quotes "Two are better than one.", which isn't the exact BSB wording.

rule.text: Quotes: Quotation marks around Bible words mean the exact BSB wording, punctuation included.

findings.problem: The setup line "it's not work yourself to the bone, and it's not do nothing either" rules out both wrong answers on card 6 ("Two handfuls with toil" and "Empty hands with rest") before the baker picks.

rule.text: A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.

findings.problem: "So it's not work yourself to the bone, and it's not do nothing either" says how verses 4, 5 and 6 connect, and the text never draws that link. It also recasts verse 4 as overwork, when the text is about labor that springs from envy.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: Stop 1 has 6 multiple choice cards, 1 true or false card and no fill in the blank cards, so multiple choice dominates the stop by a wide margin.

rule.text: No stop repeats another stop's pattern, and no type dominates a stop by a wide margin.

findings.problem: "The man finally asks himself a question" adds a time sequence. Ecclesiastes 4:8 does not say he asks it finally or at the end of anything.

rule.text: Times stay true. No time in the text means none added.

findings.problem: The card announces "three pictures", which tells the baker the content of 4:10-12, but it cites only 4:10.

rule.text: Every story card cites the verses it tells, from the first verse it uses to the last, no wider and no narrower.

findings.problem: The joke invents a new event in Papa Dorin's backstory: he tipped over in the junk drawer and stayed sideways until someone dug for tape. The allowance for jokes covers small moments around his bakery, not new events in the drawer years.

rule.text: His backstory, family, bakery and mission are the Dorinverse story in this file. He can talk about them freely, but never adds anything new to them. His jokes can make up small moments and habits around his bakery.

findings.problem: "From prison to the throne with everybody behind him" restates verses 14 and 15, which cards 12 to 14 already covered. Only the quote from 4:16 moves the passage forward, and the citation widens to 4:14-16 to cover the recap.

"And the crowd?" and "everybody behind him" present "all the people who were before them" (4:16) as the youth's followers. The text leaves open who "them" is and how those people connect to the youth.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.
